report:
**Conclusion:** Yes—*for critically ill hospitalized COVID-19 patients who need oxygen or mechanical ventilation*, a short course of a systemic corticosteroid (such as dexamethasone) **improves survival on average**. But it does **not ensure** that any individual patient survives, and it is not beneficial for every severity group.

The strongest direct evidence is the large randomized RECOVERY trial. Dexamethasone 6 mg daily for up to 10 days reduced 28-day deaths in patients already on invasive mechanical ventilation (29.3% with dexamethasone vs 41.4% with usual care; rate ratio 0.64) and in those receiving oxygen without ventilation (23.3% vs 26.2%; 0.82). That is compelling evidence of a causal mortality benefit, rather than merely an association.

A prospective WHO-coordinated meta-analysis of randomized trials in *critically ill* patients independently supported this result: systemic corticosteroids were associated with lower 28-day all-cause mortality than usual care/placebo.

The important counterevidence is also from RECOVERY: among hospitalized patients **not needing respiratory support**, deaths were numerically higher with dexamethasone (17.8% vs 14.0%; rate ratio 1.19, with uncertainty). Steroids suppress inflammation—which helps in the later, oxygen-requiring inflammatory phase—but can also impair immune responses and cause harms such as high blood glucose, delirium, and secondary infections. WHO therefore strongly recommends them for severe/critical COVID-19 but suggests against them in non-severe disease.

So your answer is substantially right if “critically ill” means oxygen-dependent or ventilated COVID-19: these drugs increase the chance of survival, but are not a guarantee and should be clinician-directed.
